home-and-zero.title: Home the machine & zero the Z axis

steps.text: Welcome to Training Mode. The machine will not move — every control is live, but a simulated tool answers instead of the real one. We'll practice the startup routine every job begins with: homing, then zeroing the Z axis.

First, the machine needs to find its fixed home position. I've put a model of the simulated machine on screen so you can watch it move. In the Console's Machine card, press the highlighted Home XY button.
Watch the tool drive toward each proximity switch, back off, and creep back in slowly for an exact reading — first X, then Y. The Inputs lights in the top bar show each switch tripping.

The DRO now reads X 0.00  Y 0.00 — the machine knows where it is. Next: the Z axis is zeroed to the top of your material using the metal touch plate. On a real machine you'd rest the plate under the bit now. Press the highlighted Home Z button.
The bit finds the plate twice — a fast touch, then a slow one for accuracy. Watch input 1 light up at each touch; Z is set from the plate's known thickness before retracting to a safe height.
That's the whole startup routine. Home XY once per session, zero the Z whenever the bit or material changes. This is exactly what you'll do on the real machine — the only difference is that it moves.

drive-the-machine.title: Drive the machine with the keypad

steps.text: Time to take the wheel. Driving the machine by hand is how you position the bit before every cut. That's your simulated tool on stage, and beside it a practice keypad — the same direction arrows you'll find on the real motion keypad.
The arrows jog the machine. Press and hold one of the XY arrows and watch the tool glide over the table. The position readout in the top bar follows along — let go and it stops instantly.
Now the fun part. Hold Z down until the Z readout goes below zero — below zero is inside the material, and the simulated bit will start carving the sheet.
You're cutting! Steer with the XY arrows and draw something — the trench follows the bit. This is exactly what happens when a job runs: Z plunges into the material, then X and Y draw the toolpath.
On a real machine you'd never drag the bit sideways out of a cut without thinking — you always retract before traveling. Hold Z up until the readout is back above zero.

That's hand-driving: jog to position, plunge only on purpose, retract before you travel. On the real dashboard these same arrows live behind the highlighted keypad button in the top bar — it will feel like an old friend.
